title: Sustainability: why it matters in projects
blurb: Explain why sustainability responsibilities, principles and priorities belong in every project, and the impact they have on its choices.
question: A council is building a new leisure centre. Gas boilers are cheaper to install, heat pumps are cheaper to run and far lower in carbon, and the council has a net-zero policy and wants local people employed on the build. Why must the project consider sustainability, and how will it affect the project's decisions?

teach.body: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. The PMQ syllabus frames it as balancing the environmental, social, economic and administrative considerations that will impact a project. In plain English: a project should not solve today's problem by creating a bigger one for the planet, the community, the organisation's finances or its future governance.

teach.caption: Sustainability is NOT only 'green'. The PMQ adds social, economic and administrative considerations.

teach.body: Legal and regulatory duties: environmental, planning and employment law. Organisational policy and ESG commitments, such as net-zero targets. Stakeholder expectations from customers, investors, staff and local communities. Reputation. Whole-life cost and resource efficiency: waste costs money. Social value, often scored in public procurement. Above all, projects are where an organisation's future footprint is decided: once a building, product or system is designed, most of its lifetime impact is fixed.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Sponsor sets objectives; PM plans them in; suppliers deliver
Whole-life thinking; minimise harm; treat people fairly
Net zero first, or local jobs first
teach.caption: Priorities come from the organisation's strategy and policies, so they differ between organisations and projects.

teach.h: Where it bites in a linear life cycle
teach.caption: Most impact is locked in early, at Concept and Definition. In an iterative life cycle, sustainability is written into backlog acceptance criteria and reviewed every iteration.

teach.body: Sustainability changes which options are considered, the design, the materials and suppliers chosen, costs and timescales, the risks faced, the benefits claimed and the success criteria. It also brings trade-offs. A lower-carbon option may cost more up front but less over its life. A local supplier may be dearer but create jobs. The sponsor decides the balance, guided by the organisation's priorities.

teach.caption: Judged on install cost alone, gas wins. Judged on whole-life cost, carbon and policy, heat pumps win.

teach.body: Riverside's sponsor also sets social priorities: contractors must offer local apprenticeships and the centre must be fully accessible. Administratively, the project follows the council's sustainability policy, records its decisions, and reports progress against its sustainability objectives to the council's cabinet. These choices add cost and some delivery risk, but they also strengthen the business case and public support.

teach.text: Exam trap 1: treating sustainability as purely environmental. The PMQ lists environmental, social, economic AND administrative considerations. Exam trap 2: treating it as something to check at the end. By handover most impacts are fixed, so it must shape options and design from the start.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define sustainability and name the four considerations: environmental, social, economic, administrative.
Explain WHY it is considered: legal duties, policy and ESG commitments, stakeholder expectations, reputation, whole-life cost.
Describe the impact on the project: options, design, materials, suppliers, costs, risks, benefits, success criteria.
Mention responsibilities and priorities: the sponsor sets objectives, the PM builds them into the plan, suppliers deliver.
Use the scenario to show a trade-off and how it is resolved.
Sustainability: meeting today's needs without compromising future generations.
PMQ balances environmental, social, economic and administrative considerations.
Drivers: law, policy and ESG, stakeholders, reputation, whole-life cost, social value.
It affects options, design, materials, suppliers, costs, risks, benefits and success criteria.
Consider it from the start: most impact is locked in at Concept and Definition.

summary: You can now define sustainability, name its four considerations and explain why projects must take account of them. You can also describe how sustainability responsibilities, principles and priorities shape a project's options, design, suppliers, costs, risks and success criteria, including the trade-offs involved.

A.q: The PMQ syllabus describes sustainability as balancing which considerations?
options: Time, cost, quality, scope and benefits
Political, economic, legal, technological
Environmental, social, economic, administrative
Strengths, weaknesses, threats, opportunities
A.why: The syllabus frames sustainability as balancing environmental, social, economic and administrative considerations that impact a project.

whyNot.0: Time, cost, quality, scope and benefits are project constraints and outcomes, not the sustainability considerations.
whyNot.1: These are PESTLE headings for analysing the external environment.
whyNot.3: These are the four elements of a SWOT analysis.

options: Meeting present needs without harming the future
Reducing a project's budget wherever possible
Using only recycled materials on every project
Making sure every output lasts as long as possible
A.why: Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

whyNot.1: Cutting budgets can harm sustainability; it is about whole-life value, not lowest cost.
whyNot.2: Recycled materials can help, but they are one tactic, not the definition.
whyNot.3: Durability can help, but sustainability is broader: environmental, social, economic and administrative.

A.q: What is the STRONGEST reason to consider sustainability from the very start of a project?
options: It is only relevant to construction projects
Options and design fix most future impacts
It can be added cheaply once delivery ends
It replaces the need for a business case
A.why: Once options are chosen and the design is set, most of the output's lifetime impact is locked in, so sustainability must shape those early decisions.

whyNot.0: Sustainability applies to all projects: IT, events, products and services as well as construction.
whyNot.2: Retrofitting sustainability after delivery is usually expensive or impossible.
whyNot.3: Sustainability objectives belong in the business case; they do not replace it.

B.q: A council requires every bidder for a new school to design it for full accessibility and community use outside school hours. Which sustainability consideration does this MAINLY address?
options: Economic
Environmental
Administrative
Social
B.why: Accessibility and community use are about people and communities: the social consideration.

whyNot.0: Economic covers whole-life cost and long-term financial viability.
whyNot.1: Environmental covers carbon, energy, waste and nature.
whyNot.2: Administrative covers governance, policy, compliance and reporting.

B.q: Riverside's heat pumps cost more to install than gas boilers but much less to run. Why might the sponsor still choose them?
options: Upfront cost is all a business case considers
Lower whole-life cost and carbon fit the policy
Heat pumps remove the need for maintenance
Installing them shortens the project schedule
B.why: Over the building's life, heat pumps cost less and emit far less carbon, which fits the council's net-zero policy.

whyNot.0: A business case should consider whole-life costs and benefits, not just installation cost.
whyNot.2: Heat pumps still need maintenance; that is not the reason.
whyNot.3: There is no reason to expect a shorter schedule; new supply chains may even lengthen it.

B.q:
Which TWO are typical reasons for considering sustainability in a project?
1) Legal and regulatory duties
2) Stakeholder and investor expectations
3) Removing the need for risk management
4) Guaranteeing the lowest capital cost
options: 2 and 3
1 and 4
1 and 2
3 and 4
B.why: Legal duties and stakeholder expectations are two of the main drivers for considering sustainability.

whyNot.0: Stakeholder expectations are right, but sustainability adds risks to manage rather than removing risk management.
whyNot.1: Legal duties are right, but sustainable options often cost more up front.
whyNot.3: Neither is true: risk management is still needed and the lowest capital cost is not guaranteed.

C.q: On a hospital car park project, the cheapest contractor would bring in a distant workforce, while a slightly dearer one would hire locally. What does this MOST clearly illustrate?
options: A trade-off between sustainability pillars
A failure of the project's change control
A sign that sustainability does not apply
A risk that should be transferred to users
C.why: Lower cost (economic) competes with local employment (social). The sponsor must balance them using the organisation's priorities.

whyNot.1: Change control manages changes to an agreed baseline; this is a selection decision.
whyNot.2: This is a sustainability decision: it involves economic and social considerations.
whyNot.3: This is a choice to make, not a risk to transfer, and users would not be the right owner.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical way sustainability affects a project?
options: It shapes which options are appraised
It informs material and supplier choices
It adds to the risks and success criteria
It removes the need to consider cost
C.why: Sustainability does not remove cost from the decision. Economic sustainability is one of the four considerations, and whole-life cost matters.

whyNot.0: Sustainability objectives change which options are worth appraising.
whyNot.1: Material and supplier choices are among the biggest sustainability decisions.
whyNot.2: Sustainability brings new risks and often new success criteria.

C.q: A business case states: 'sustainability will be reviewed after handover'. What is the MAIN weakness of this approach?
options: Sustainability is only a legal matter
Key impacts are locked in by then
Handover reviews are not permitted
Users cannot comment on sustainability
C.why: By handover the options, design, materials and suppliers have been chosen, so most impacts can no longer be changed cheaply.

whyNot.0: Law is only one driver; policy, stakeholders and whole-life cost matter too.
whyNot.2: Post-handover reviews are allowed; the problem is that they come too late to shape the decisions.
whyNot.3: Users can and should comment; that is not the weakness here.

reteach.title: Renovating a family home
reteach.question: A family is renovating an old house. They could fit the cheapest boiler, skip the loft insulation and put all the rubble in one skip. What would a sustainable renovation look like, using the four considerations?

blocks.body: Environmental: does it cut energy use and waste? Social: are the neighbours kept informed, and are local tradespeople used? Economic: is the efficient boiler cheaper over 15 years, even if it costs more now? Administrative: are building control approvals, certificates and receipts in order, so the house can be sold later? A cheap renovation that fails on these can cost far more in the long run.

blocks.h: A common principle: the waste hierarchy

blocks.text: The decision that matters most is made before any work starts: the design and the choice of boiler. Recycling the skip at the end is good, but it cannot undo a poor design.

explain.body: Environmental (carbon, energy, waste), social (people and communities), economic (whole-life cost and viability) and administrative (governance, policy, compliance and reporting).

test.q: Which sustainability consideration covers governance, policies, compliance and how sustainability is managed and reported?
options: Environmental
Social
Administrative
Economic
test.why: The administrative consideration covers governance, policy, compliance and reporting.

whyNot.0: Environmental covers carbon, energy, waste and nature.
whyNot.3: Economic covers whole-life cost and long-term viability.

explain.body: Legal duties, organisational policy and ESG commitments, stakeholder and investor expectations, reputation, whole-life cost and resource efficiency, net-zero targets and social value in procurement.

test.q: A listed company's investors expect every major project to show its carbon impact. Which driver for sustainability does this represent?
options: Stakeholder expectations
Schedule optimisation
Technical design assurance
Quality control checks
test.why: Investors are stakeholders, and their expectations are a major driver for considering sustainability.

whyNot.1: Schedule optimisation (such as crashing or fast-tracking) is about time, not why sustainability matters.
whyNot.2: Technical design assurance checks the solution's design, not investor expectations.
whyNot.3: Quality control checks outputs against requirements.

explain.body: The sponsor sets sustainability objectives in the business case, guided by organisational policy. The project manager builds them into the plan and controls them. The team and suppliers deliver them day to day.

test.q: Who normally sets a project's sustainability objectives in the business case?
options: Each supplier, in its bid
The project team members
The end users at handover
The sponsor, from policy
test.why: The sponsor owns the business case and sets its sustainability objectives in line with organisational policy.

whyNot.0: Suppliers respond to the client's objectives; they do not set them.
whyNot.1: The team delivers objectives; it does not set them.
whyNot.2: By handover it is far too late to set objectives.

explain.body: In a linear life cycle, set objectives at Concept and design them in at Definition. In an iterative life cycle, add sustainability to backlog acceptance criteria so every iteration is checked against it.

test.q: In an iterative project, how can sustainability BEST be built into delivery?
options: Assess it only once, after the last release
Include it in backlog acceptance criteria
Leave it to the next product owner
Treat it as out of scope for software
test.why: Writing sustainability into acceptance criteria means every iteration's work is checked against it.

whyNot.0: Assessing only at the end is too late to influence what was built.
whyNot.2: Deferring it to a future role leaves it unmanaged now.
whyNot.3: Software has sustainability impacts too, such as energy use and accessibility.
